Structure, evidence, and how you recover. Never the accent.
Blaming somebody else, a story that changes, and answers that never end.
How will you compare the final two, and what would make you say no to me?
The second round is with somebody you have not met, and I cannot tell you who.
That is fine. Could I ask what they will be scoring?
Structure, evidence, and consistency with the first round. They have the notes.
So the risk is not a hard question. The risk is a different version of the same answer.
That is exactly the risk, and it is the most common red flag in my files.
Then I will give the same figures I gave you, even when they sound rehearsed.
Say the numbers slowly, and let them write. One more thing: they will ask what would make you say no to us.
I have an honest answer to that, and I would rather give it than a polite one.
Good. The ones who hold up are the ones who are the same person twice.
It is the same answer I gave in the first round, and the same figure.
Could I ask what you will be scoring today?
Let me give you the number first, and then the reasoning.
What would make you say no to me?
I would say no to this if the reporting line went through somebody else.

People imagine the scorecard is about language, and it never is. Ours has four lines. Structure: does the answer have a shape, or does it wander until the candidate runs out of air. Evidence: is there a number, a date or a name in it. Recovery: what happens after a question that does not go well, because something always does not go well. And consistency: is this the same story we heard in the first round, with the same figures. That last line is where most people lose points, and almost nobody prepares for it. They prepare new material instead, which is exactly the wrong instinct. If your first answer was good, give the same one. We are not bored. We are checking.

At the end I ask every candidate the same thing: what would make you say no to us. Most of them tell me there is nothing, and that answer costs them. It tells me either that they have not thought about it, or that they will say anything to get the offer, and I do not want either of those people running my finance function. The answers I remember are specific. One man told me he would say no if the reporting line to the board went through somebody else, because he had lived that once. I disagreed with him about the structure, and I hired him anyway, because I knew exactly what I was getting. Say the true thing. It is the only answer in that conversation that cannot be checked, and it is the one I trust.
